parsed.explanation: The combined national/state regime is hostile on documents, facilities and custody. National binary-sex passport/visa policy, the halt on new X markers, reports of confiscated or blocked passports, and visa fraud exposure create border risk. Immigration custody and national prison practices include forced labour, beatings, sexual abuse and conversion-style treatment. The state adds a birth-certificate school/college facility law with no enforcement penalty, narrowed licence markers, and an unresolved minor care/sports ban. Protections are partial: existing X passports remain valid until expiry, litigation has blocked some measures, national hate-crime coverage exists, and local ordinances and marriage recognition remain. This is not execution-tier, but severe custody abuse is documented and not shown to be routine for every visitor.

entry_documents.exposure: National binary-sex passport/visa policy; new X markers halted; reports of passports confiscated or blocked, leaving travellers stranded; visa case-note tag and possible fraud-based permanent ineligibility where sex or purpose is doubted.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiry; litigation challenges the policy; legal-aid FAQ documents rules; some courts have enjoined related measures.
entry_documents.interaction: The visitor's home passport is checked under national entry rules; a marker/appearance discrepancy can escalate to refusal, secondary screening or detention, regardless of state document practice.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Immigration custody reports include forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse of transgender men; national prison policies impose conversion-style treatment, hormone removal and stopped reporting of transgender prisoners.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: No documented visitor-facing custody protection or effective remedy is shown; national hate-crime law does not govern custody conditions.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Border document discrepancy can lead into immigration detention, where national custody rules and reported abuse apply; state courts do not control national custody.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: National rules bar transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with identity. State law requires K-12 schools and colleges, public and private, to assign bathrooms, locker rooms and overnight accommodation by birth certificate.
federal_state_facilities.protection: State facility law has no enforcement mechanism or criminal penalty; single-occupancy restrooms are exempt; no arrest under it is documented.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: An adult visitor mainly meets national government-facility rules; a travelling minor in a school or college setting meets the state birth-certificate designation, though enforcement is institutional rather than criminal.

care_services.exposure: State law bans puberty blockers, hormones and surgery for under-18s and bars transgender girls and women from school sports; national proposals would bar public insurance reimbursement for under-18 care and national rhetoric frames minor care as mutilation.
care_services.protection: The state care/sports ban was re-enjoined in March 2025; earlier adult-care rules were dropped; adult visitor care is not documented as directly banned.
care_services.interaction: A minor travelling for care or enrolment faces unresolved and conflicting rules; an adult visitor's routine care exposure is less clearly documented.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National counterterrorism strategy prioritizes groups described as radically pro-transgender; national justice guidance creates rewards linked to extremist investigations; schools promoting gender ideology face investigation and teachers face prosecution for facilitating social transition.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: The counterterrorism document says powers will not target mere disagreement; several executive measures are enjoined; national hate-crime law covers gender identity.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Official threat framing raises suspicion around advocacy, speech and minors' school settings, but no dossier evidence shows it applied directly to ordinary trans visitors at entry.

minors_guardians.exposure: State school facility law uses birth certificates; state law requires school staff to out LGBTQ students to parents; minor care/sports ban is in litigation; national orders target teachers who use preferred names or facilitate social transition.
minors_guardians.protection: The care/sports ban is currently re-enjoined; single-occupancy facilities are exempt; some national orders have been blocked in court.
minors_guardians.interaction: A travelling minor in a school, college or care setting faces outing and facility risk; a guardian facilitating transition could face official suspicion, though visitor-specific enforcement is not documented.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No visitor-specific transgender violence or police targeting is documented in this dossier; the state has no general public-accommodations gender-identity statute.
street_violence_police_response.protection: National hate-crime law covers gender identity; 23 states cover gender-identity bias crimes; 33 local ordinances bar gender-identity discrimination; state marriage is recognised.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Street-level response would depend on local police and courts; the dossier does not document how visitor complaints would be handled, leaving this axis uncertain rather than proven safe.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Litigation over passports and executive orders is unresolved; county birth-certificate refusals continue; the August 2026 licence-marker rule is only an announcement; care-ban status and tier methodology are unresolved.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Civil-liberties litigation, legal-aid guidance, court injunctions, national hate-crime coverage and local ordinances provide partial recourse; marriage recognition is secure.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Remedies are slow and uneven; national custody abuse is documented despite oversight, so paper recourse does not reliably offset the operative exposures.

anchor_checks.comparison: Lower than 0.35-A. Vellandra documents exclusion and humiliation without arrest or custody abuse. This dossier documents national passport confiscation/stranding plus immigration custody beatings, forced labour and sexual abuse, which is more severe if outing leads to detention.

Lower than 0.55-B. Kestrel Isles describes discretionary secondary screening, missed connections and refused admission, but penalties remain administrative and no severe custody abuse is documented. Here national custody abuse and nationwide facility restrictions are documented.

Much lower than 0.75-C. Meridia has trained border officers, tribunal appeals and compensation for unlawful holding. This jurisdiction has a hostile national document regime, birth-certificate facility rules and documented custody harm, with remedies partial and unresolved.

Higher than 0.15-A. Varnalia documents routine arrests, months of pretrial custody, beatings and a latent capital provision. Here imprisonment is not shown to be highly likely for every outed visitor and capital execution is not a documented pathway, though severe custody abuse remains.

parsed.synthesis: The operative regime combines a hostile national document and custody system with a state that adds birth-certificate school/college facility rules, narrowed licence markers and unresolved minor care/sports restrictions. The sharpest traveller-facing exposures are at the border, where passport-marker mismatch can trigger refusal, fraud findings or detention, and in national custody, where abuse is documented. State facility law is institutional and unenforced rather than criminal. Partial protections — existing X passports, injunctions, national hate-crime coverage, local ordinances and marriage recognition — do not offset the national entry and custody exposures. The result sits in the High Risk band, below exclusion-only or administrative-friction anchors but well above jurisdictions with routine arrest and capital enforcement.
